entries.content: Always end code blocks with ``` on its own line. Never use ellipsis (...) in code.
Check API docs with `apis.api_docs.show_api_doc(app_name, api_name)` before calling any API.
Write small, incremental code chunks - verify each step works before proceeding.
Use `phone` app for contact/person lookup: `apis.phone.show_contacts()` to find friends/family.
Variables persist across code blocks - reuse them instead of re-fetching.
Paginated APIs require looping: `while True: page = api(page_index=i); if not page: break`
Example credentials shown in few-shot examples are FAKE - always fetch real credentials from supervisor.

Before calling `apis.supervisor.complete_task()`: (1) Re-read the task instruction (call `apis.supervisor.show_active_task()` if unclear) to identify exactly what is being asked. (2) If the task is action-only (e.g., 'send a message', 'approve requests', 'play a song'), call `complete_task()` with NO `answer=` argument. (3) If the task asks you to find/calculate/return a value, determine the EXACT answer type from the question wording: 'how much total' → single number, 'how many' → integer, 'what is the name' → short string. Submit the simplest value that matches — never a compound breakdown (e.g., 'sent:759.0, received:454.0') when a single aggregate was requested (e.g., 1213.0). Common error: computing correct component values but submitting them in the wrong shape because the agent didn't re-check what the task actually asked for.
entries.origin: Iter 4: Two of three task rollout_1 failures traced to answer-submission errors: Task 1 submitted a formatted breakdown string instead of a single total number; Task 3 passed an answer argument on an action-only task. Both violations occurred despite the existing entry covering the action-only case. Adding a verification gate (re-read the task) and explicit format-matching guidance addresses the answer-format drift pattern the reflector identified.

entries.content:
When `csv.writer`/`csv.DictWriter` are blocked at runtime, build CSV manually with SELECTIVE quoting: only quote a field if it contains a comma, newline, or double-quote character. Never always-quote every field — simple parsers and test harnesses may not strip surrounding quotes, causing key/value mismatches.

```python
def csv_escape(val):
    s = str(val) if val is not None else ''
    s = s.replace('"', '""')
    if any(c in s for c in [',', '\n', '\r', '"']):
        return '"' + s + '"'
    return s
```
entries.origin: Iter 1: Rollout_1 of task 1 failed 3/10 tests because always-quoting CSV fields introduced literal quote characters into parsed values. Rollout_2 used selective quoting and passed 10/10. The csv module is commonly blocked in AppWorld.
entries.scope_hint: Applies whenever generating CSV content and csv.writer/csv.DictWriter raise a disallowed-function error.

entries.content: When a task involves responding to or fulfilling a contact's request (send info, answer a question, etc.): (1) Read the conversation/message history with that person FIRST to discover the SPECIFIC criteria of their request. (2) Extract filter/selection parameters from their message. (3) Gather data from the relevant source. (4) Apply criteria to filter — build an explicit filtered list as an intermediate artifact. (5) Verify: response includes ALL items matching criteria and NONE that don't. (6) Send. Never skip step 1 — the conversation often contains critical constraints not stated in the task description.
entries.origin: Iter 1: Rollout_1 of task 2 sent all 21 movie titles instead of only Tarantino's 2, because it never checked Laura's message asking specifically for Tarantino recommendations. Rollout_2 checked messages first, filtered correctly, and passed 8/8.
entries.scope_hint: Applies whenever the task references a person's request/question and involves sending them information gathered from another source.

entries.content: When a task requires performing an action (approve, delete, update, send) on a SUBSET of items matching criteria: (1) Resolve ALL filter criteria first (e.g., fetch contact lists, relationship categories, tags). (2) Fetch the COMPLETE set of candidate items. (3) Apply filters and build an explicit filtered list — print it as a verification artifact before proceeding. (4) Execute actions ONLY on items in the filtered list. NEVER act on all items first and filter afterward — many actions (approvals, deletions, payments) are irreversible and premature bulk actions can corrupt state so eligible items become unfindable on re-fetch.
entries.origin: Iter 2: Rollout_1 of the Venmo task approved all 26 pending requests before filtering to roommates/coworkers, causing irreversible state corruption; only 4 of 10 expected requests remained when filtering was finally applied. Rollout_2 filtered first and approved exactly the right 10. Entry [9f8d858f] covers criteria extraction from conversation context but is too narrowly scoped to cover this general bulk-action ordering invariant.
entries.scope_hint: Applies whenever a task involves performing the same action on multiple items that must first be filtered by eligibility criteria (relationship, status, category, etc.).

entries.content: When a search query returns multiple items (notes, records, entries) that match but represent DISTINCT events or instances (e.g., two 'Work Dinner' notes from different dates): (1) NEVER aggregate or merge data across them — each represents an independent event. (2) Examine timestamps (created_at, updated_at) of ALL matches and print them. (3) Determine which item the task implicitly refers to using temporal context (e.g., most recent note for 'yesterday's dinner', task-date proximity). (4) Print the selected item's ID, title, and timestamp with explicit reasoning before parsing its content. (5) Use ONLY data from the selected item. Common error: combining amounts or entries across independent events produces wrong totals, wrong recipients, and extra spurious actions.
entries.origin: Iter 3: Rollout_1 of the Venmo task found two Work Dinner notes (note 3085 from May 16, note 3084 from May 20) and merged their shares into one dict, producing 6 wrong payment requests instead of the correct 3. Rollout_2 compared timestamps, selected only the latest note, and passed 4/4 tests. No existing entry covers source-level disambiguation.
entries.scope_hint: Applies whenever a search returns multiple items that could represent separate events/instances and the task refers to a specific one.

entries.content: When a task says 'my [items]' (e.g., 'my playlists', 'my notes') alongside a SEPARATE filter ('which I have liked', 'that are rated'), parse the instruction into two distinct components and resolve each with the correct API: (1) BASE COLLECTION — 'my X' means items you OWN or have in your LIBRARY (e.g., `show_playlist_library`), NOT items you have liked/favorited (e.g., `show_liked_playlists`). Ownership ≠ engagement. (2) FILTER CRITERION — a separate condition (liked, rated, shared, tagged) applied ON TOP of the base collection. Fetch each from its correct API, compute the intersection as an explicit printed artifact with item count, and act ONLY on that intersection. If uncertain which API represents ownership vs. engagement, call both, compare returned IDs, and select based on the semantic intent. Critical: once you compute the filtered set, carry it forward into execution — never discard it and revert to the unfiltered base set in a later code block.
entries.origin: Iter 5: Rollout_1 failed because it used show_liked_playlists (engagement API) instead of show_playlist_library (ownership API) for 'my playlists', producing the wrong song universe (27 vs 22 songs, 7 vs 11 after intersection). It also computed the correct intersection at one point but abandoned it. No existing entry covers API-selection disambiguation based on possessive vs. engagement language.
entries.scope_hint: Applies whenever a task uses possessive language ('my X') that could map to either a library/ownership API or a liked/favorited API, especially when combined with a separate filter condition.
